title: Social teaching close
hook: love of neighbor, built into how we live together

segments.voice: Yesterday, social teaching at home: the big letters weighed in small choices. Your line was conscience at the checkout. Which habit did you hold up to the light? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

A bridge carries strangers across a river all day long, and hardly anyone crossing it thinks about it. Somebody did, once. Somebody calculated the load, the wind, the winter, so that people they would never meet could get home safely. That's a kind of care that doesn't look like care. It looks like steel and paperwork. This block of the path began with a phrase, love, organized, and it ends today with a picture very close to that bridge: love of neighbor, built into the way people live together.
screen: `A BRIDGE FULL OF STRANGERS.` → `CARE THAT LOOKS LIKE STEEL.` → `LOVE, BUILT IN.`

segments.voice: First, the old command. Paul writes to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." One person carrying another's load. Catholic social teaching keeps asking a second question: what if the load could be made lighter for everyone, before anyone has to carry it alone? Second, two ways to love. Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote that there is the love of one neighbor, face to face, and also an institutional path of charity, where love works through law, economics and politics for the common good. He called that second path no less a form of love than the first. Pope Francis, for his part, speaks of political love, the love that builds a fairer society for people one will never meet. Third, what the block has added up to. Every life. Everyone takes part. Rights and duties. The poor first. Work has dignity. One family. Our common home. Markets have limits. Nothing and no one thrown away. Each one is love of neighbor, set into something that lasts longer than a single good deed. Fourth, what it doesn't replace. Benedict was clear that no structure will ever make person-to-person love unnecessary. There will always be someone lonely, someone grieving, someone who needs a face, not a policy. So the Church asks for both: the hand on the shoulder, and the bridge. Love made structural isn't love made cold. It's love that keeps working after you've gone home.
screen: `BEAR YE ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.` · `FACE TO FACE, AND THROUGH INSTITUTIONS.` · `THE BLOCK'S LINES, ADDED UP.` · `STRUCTURES NEVER REPLACE A FACE.` · then, large: `SO YOU SHALL FULFIL THE LAW OF CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: commit to one ongoing act. Settle, and breathe. Let the block's lines pass by slowly, and notice which one stays. The poor first. Our common home. Everyone takes part. Then pick one act that could keep going without you having to decide it fresh each time. A monthly gift set up once. A regular shift somewhere. A letter to a representative, with a reminder to write another. Something small that lasts. Hold it. If you pray, you can offer it to God as a promise. The bell holds the time.

Social teaching close. The block in one picture: love of neighbor, face to face and built into how we live together. Tomorrow a new block begins, on Mary: her feasts, her titles, and what the Church teaches about her. Today's word.
Your line: love made structural. Today, set up the ongoing act you chose, so that it keeps happening even on the days you forget. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics live social teaching both in direct works of mercy and in longer commitments: volunteering on a schedule, giving regularly, joining parish justice groups, and taking part in public life with the Church's principles in mind.

fork.setup: your street floods every spring and the same neighbors lose everything. you've helped bail out basements for years. what does love made structural add?
options: keep helping, and push for a drain that stops the flood.
fork.reveal: the Church asks for both: the hand on the shoulder now, and the structure that lightens the load for everyone.

trapdoor: what you thought: social teaching is a list of rules about politics.
what it means: love of neighbor, built into how people live together, beside face-to-face love.
what a scholar hears: Benedict XVI's institutional path of charity in Caritas in Veritate, and Francis's political love in Fratelli Tutti.

sources.quoted: Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ.

notes: Caritas in Veritate §7 paraphrased: the 'institutional path' of charity, 'no less excellent and effective' than direct charity. Confirm.
Deus Caritas Est §28b paraphrased: there will always be suffering and loneliness that call for personal love; no just order makes charity superfluous. Confirm.
Fratelli Tutti §§180–182 paraphrased on political love / social love. Confirm section numbers.

Block D close: the teach names a selection of the block's carries (every life, everyone takes part, rights and duties, the poor first, work has dignity, one family, our common home, markets have limits, nothing and no one thrown away), not all of them.
Editor pass: 'Pope Francis goes further' changed to 'for his part', so the two popes are not ranked.
